standard.title: Express Emotions
standard.description: express and describe emotions they experience
standard.prior_knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students have intuitive emotional experience but limited vocabulary and structured practice for identifying and expressing emotions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students express and describe emotions they experience using appropriate language and actions, and make connections between feelings, body reactions and body language.

nodes.label: Naming emotions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and name a range of emotions — happy, sad, excited, tired, angry, scared, confused — and describe what they look like in others and themselves.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least four emotions and describe what they look like (facial expression, body language) in a character, image or peer.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe a range of emotions (at least six) in stories, images and peers; connect emotion names with observable indicators (expression, posture, voice); recall emotional responses to their own experiences.
wider: Explore how emotions are expressed differently across cultures — using stories or examples from First Nations Australian or Asian cultural contexts
Investigate emotion expression in physical activity contexts — e.g. how winning, losing or taking risks feels
Represent a range of emotions through movement, drawing or creative expression
nodes.hinge_reason: Emotion vocabulary is prerequisite for expressing and communicating feelings (next node). Students with limited emotion vocabulary cannot access appropriate language or actions for communicating their feelings in different situations.

response_modes.reason: Emotion vocabulary is genuinely a repertoire — more named emotions means more precise communication. Accumulate the range systematically through stories, imagery and physical activity reflection.
Emotions in varied contexts — stories, movement, cultural settings — broaden recognition beyond the classroom's dominant emotional register.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-cultural and physical activity emotion contexts are genuinely rich — they reveal that emotional expression is situational and culturally shaped, not just personal.
success_criteria: Names at least four emotions correctly when shown or described a scenario
Describes at least one observable indicator (expression, posture, voice) for two different emotions

nodes.label: Communicating emotions appropriately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use appropriate language and actions to communicate their feelings in different situations, and connect feelings to body reactions and body language.
nodes.minimum_width: Use words or gestures to communicate one feeling in a social or play context in a way that is appropriate for the situation.
nodes.typical_width: Practise and refine appropriate emotional communication in a range of situations; make connections between feelings, body reactions (heart racing, stomach butterflies) and visible body language; share emotional responses to experiences in a variety of ways.
wider: Explore and practise communicating emotions in challenging situations — adventures, risks or emergencies in stories
Connect body reactions during physical activity (breathlessness, energy) to emotional states
Discuss how expressing emotions helps social connection and conflict resolution

response_modes.reason: Appropriate emotional communication is a practised skill — Foundation students need repeated, safe opportunities to try emotion vocabulary and receive affirming feedback before it becomes reliable.

success_criteria: Uses appropriate language or gesture to communicate a feeling in at least one situation
Makes a simple connection between a feeling and a body reaction or body language signal
